notes: PROPOSED--"We have received several reports of the spray plumbing from the pump to the on-off valve blowing off the pump after the stainless safety wire fails that is designed to prevent such occurrences. It has also been brought to our attention that the plumbing is susceptible to blowing off at the spray valve as well as at the pump. Since this results in loss of the chemical load, the factory recommends that owners check to see that the hose clamps are tight and double up the safety wire which connects the plumbing to the pump. Owners operating AT-502/AT-502A aircraft thru s/n 502-0196 are referred to Service Letter #109 and Service Letter #114 for additional information."--PROPOSED

sections.title: Horizontal Stabilizers
notes: INSERT Figure 2-57 Horizontal Stabilizer

PROPOSED--"Reports have been received of large birds striking the outboard end of the horizontal tail on various aircraft. In a few cases, the bird impacted near the gap between the elevator horn and the horizontal stabilizer. The damaged surface was pushed into the gap and caused the elevator horn to become obstructed. To help prevent the likelihood of jamming, Air Tractor is installing perforated ribs in the elevators and stabilizers of new aircraft.

Air Tractor recommends that all operators, especially those who operate in areas where impact with large birds are likely to have their aircraft modified to perforate the ribs of this area. The perforated ribs will allow the unsupported tip of the nose rib to break free if it becomes damaged and reduce the risk of binding. This change will also remove two non-structural closeout plates on those aircraft that have them installed. Refer to Service Letter #319 for additional information."--PROPOSED

sections.title: Rudder
notes: INSERT FIGURE Figure 2-64 Rudder The bearings exhibit little wear, but if it is necessary to replace them, construct a puller that will apply force to the outer ring of the bearing with an opposing force against the aluminum housing. Insert a AN bolt through both parts of the puller and tighten it until the bearing rim is pulled past the stake marks and the bearing comes out of the housing. Use a center punch to restake the new bearing after installation in the aluminum housing. The rudder horn has two bushings installed for wear at the cable attachment. The horn is attached to the rudder assembly with two AN stainless steel bolts. Rudder control stops are at the rudder horn. Control limits are shown in the Type Certificate Data sheet and below for reference: Left: 21° ± 1.0° Right: 21° ± 1.0° It is recommended that the cable guard be and remain installed on all aircraft. Aircraft damage due to a loose rudder cable may occur as the loss of the cable attaching hardware. Abrasion of the cotter pin from spray materials may lead to a complete loss of the attaching bolt and nut. Air Tractor has developed a stainless steel guard to the rudder cable attach hardware to prevent such a recurrence. Paragraphs edited to remove part numbers. sections.title: Fuel System Drains
notes: PROPOSED--"For AT-502A-3103 & prior (only aircraft w/ PT6A-140AG engine); AT-502B-3050 & prior; and AT-504-4028 & prior we have become aware that the fuel drain valve on the bottom of the firewall mounted fuel filter has the potential to become damaged in flight. This damage most likely would come from a bird strike on the fuel drain valve. If an object such as a bird were to hit the drain valve in flight with enough force it could be broken or cracked and leak fuel. If a leak occurred, it is also possible that air would be sucked into the fuel system. Air sucked into the fuel system could cause a loss of engine power and the engine may flame out. To prevent an occurrence as described here, a deflector/guard for the drain valve has been designed that is fully described in Service Letter #343."--PROPOSED FOR INSERTION TO INCORPORATE SL#343.

sections.title: Tail Gear Spring
notes: INSERT FIGURE Figure 2-180 Tail-Gear Spring The tail gear spring is machined of E4340 aircraft quality steel, formed, heat-treated and shotpeened for fatigue resistance. It is sandblasted and primed with an epoxy primer and finished with polyurethane paint. The forward attachment of the spring to the fuselage frame is with an AN bolt. It is clamped at the rear attachment with a clamp block which attaches to the fuselage frame with two AN bolts. There is an aluminum pad that is installed between the clamp block and the spring to allow the spring to work without putting secondary loads into the fuselage frame or attach bolts. There are square stainless shims and on occasion a spacer washer located between the clamp block and the fuselage frame. Per Section 3.1.9, during 12-month inspections the tail gear should be jacked at the stabilizer strut fittings as described under Section 2.0.4 and the tail spring checked for looseness at the clamp block. Looseness can be eliminated by removing one or more of the shims from under the clamp block. With the clamp block removed, also check the aluminum pad for condition. Some early production aircraft used AN bolts in the clamp block for the tail spring. It is also possible that a tail spring safety cable is not installed. If your aircraft does not have NAS bolts in the clamp block or have the safety cable installed, it is recommended that the operator do so according to the information in Service Letter #169. Besides saving a possible fatigue failure, the forward bolt tends to freeze up if not changed often. Be sure to grease the bolt and lightly torque the nut to XXX ft-lb. Do not overtighten as the spring must move on the bolt. Torque the clamp bolts to XXX inch-pounds (torque wrench on bolt head), and make sure there are sufficient shims between the clamp block and the fuselage frame to prevent bending the clamp block as the bolts are torqued. The tail gear spring will fatigue and break at the same point in the life of the aircraft. The number of hours before failure will vary considerably as some operators make many more landings per flight hour than others, or carry heavier loads, or operate from very rough strips. Pilot technique is a factor also, since some pilots are very rough on airplanes. See Section 6 for the fatigue life of the tail gear spring. Destruction of the old spring with a cutting torch is recommended. Part numbers have been removed. Torque values should be verified.
